common_name: Black Knight Sweet Pea (Deep Maroon Heirloom Grandiflora)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, training the twining tendrils onto a trellis or netting. Dating to the late 1890s, Black Knight is one of the oldest surviving named sweet pea cultivars and remains popular for its small but intensely dark maroon-purple standards and wings, a color so deep it reads as near-black in low light, paired with the strong, old-fashioned sweet pea perfume typical of pre-Spencer varieties. The blooms are smaller and less ruffled than modern grandiflora types, but the near-black color is unmatched among sweet peas and makes a striking contrast in mixed bouquets. Pick regularly to keep vines flowering, since seed pod formation halts further bloom.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, training the twining tendrils onto a trellis or netting. Introduced in the mid-1890s, America is a heavily streaked heirloom with crimson-red flashes and flecks laid over a white ground, giving each bloom an irregular, hand-painted candy-cane look, and it carries the strong, sweet old-fashioned fragrance typical of pre-Spencer varieties. Because the striping pattern can vary bloom to bloom, plantings show a lively range of red-and-white patterning rather than uniform color. As with other sweet peas, harvest flowers frequently for bouquets to delay seed set and extend the cool-season bloom period.

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; this is the original very dwarf, near-prostrate sweet pea, a natural mutation first recorded in 1893.

directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. First discovered as a spontaneous dwarf sport in 1893, Cupid is the ancestor of all later bush and dwarf sweet peas, forming a low, spreading, almost prostrate mat only a few inches tall but trailing well over a foot wide, studded with small, fragrant white or pink-and-white blooms. Its ground-hugging habit suits edging, rock gardens, and container spillover where taller vining types would need staking. Keep the shallow root run evenly moist and pick flowers often to prolong the cool-season display.

common_name: Gwendoline Sweet Pea (Pink Bicolor Exhibition Spencer)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Gwendoline is a long-established exhibition Spencer variety prized on the show bench for its large, well-waved blooms of soft rose-pink shading to a paler cream-pink base, carried four to a stem on long, strong stalks that are ideal for cutting. It combines good fragrance with the frilled, ruffled petal form typical of Spencer sweet peas and has remained a favorite among exhibitors for its reliable form and vigor. Pick blooms regularly to prevent seed pod formation and keep the vines flowering through the cool season.

common_name: Charlie's Angel Sweet Pea (Light Blue Ruffled Spencer)

planting.note: Direct sow as early as the soil can be worked in late winter, or in fall in mild-winter zones for a late winter to spring bloom; provide a trellis for the twining tendrils to climb.

directions: Direct sow in cool weather in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun, providing a trellis or netting for the twining tendrils to climb. Charlie's Angel is a popular modern Spencer variety bearing large, heavily waved, clear light blue flowers on long stems well suited to exhibition and cutting, with a fragrance milder than heirloom types but still noticeable up close. Its clean, true blue color and strong stem length make it a favorite for cut-flower growers wanting an alternative to the more common lavender and mauve blue tones. Pick blooms often to prevent seed pod set and extend flowering through the cool growing season.

planting.note: Sow in early spring as soon as the soil can be worked; Snoopea has tendrils replaced by extra foliage, so plants form a self-supporting mound instead of climbing.

directions: Soak seeds overnight and direct sow 1 inch deep in cool, moist soil in early spring. Snoopea is a tendril-less (semi-leafless) selection in which the twining tendrils are replaced by additional leaflets, producing a dense, mounding, self-supporting plant that needs no staking or trellis, unlike traditional vining sweet peas. It bears a full-color mix of fragrant blooms held just above the mounded foliage, making it well suited to containers, hanging baskets, and border edging where a trellis would be impractical. Deadhead or cut flowers regularly to keep the compact mound blooming through the cool season.
